leads.summary: The updated description overstates Mise trust revocation for user-configured trusted paths
leads.consequence: If the user explicitly trusts ~/Work through MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS or trusted_config_paths, rerunning the renamed migration removes the persisted grant and reports that the custom config was revoked, but Mise still applies the custom config. The description's unconditional 'is untrusted once more' is false in this supported user-override case; qualify it or explain the exception. This behavior predates the rename, so it is a description/premise correction, not a newly introduced implementation defect.

leads.summary: The revised description says a stock Work config is unchanged, but rerun deletes a restored stock config
leads.consequence: If an account ran the cleanup once and later restored the exact stock ~/Work/.mise.toml, the new migration ID causes a second run that removes the restored file, rather than leaving it unchanged. Clarify that an already-removed stock config stays absent; a recreated exact stock file is deleted on rerun. No code change requested.

comment:
## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

Follow-up to the [earlier review](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/12174#issuecomment-5836720871) and the [author reply](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/12174#issuecomment-5846470992). The head is unchanged at `72c37a91`, and current `quattro` is now `3faafba2`.

**Resolved:** the updated description now covers both re-run groups. Accounts that hold only the PTL-era marker run the cleanup for the first time. For accounts that already ran it, re-runs on `quattro` with this PR merged showed that a stock config removed by the first run stays absent, and that a custom Work config re-trusted with `mise trust` (as the migration's message invites) is untrusted again. Trust granted through mise's `trusted_config_paths` setting or `MISE_TRUSTED_CONFIG_PATHS` survives the untrust under either id, while the migration still prints that trust was revoked. That is existing behaviour of the cleanup, not an effect of the rename.

**Verified:** the earlier verified results still hold on current `quattro`. The Mise cleanup still ships there as `migrations/1789095456.sh`, identical to this PR's renamed file. None of the migration runner, provisioning, the Mise and kernel tests or the `omarchy-pkg-*` helpers changed since the earlier review. No new migration uses either id. With the PTL-era marker, `quattro` leaves the migration un-run and the stock Work config in place. `quattro` with this PR runs `1789584463.sh` and removes that config. The head merges cleanly into current `quattro`, and `mise-work-path-test.sh` passes on the merged tree. The context paragraph added to the description is accurate. Open #13365 and #13061 each fix the kernel test's pacman stub, and with #13365 that test passes with or without this rename.

### Open #11322 reuses `migrations/1789095456.sh` for a different migration

Open #11322 adds its own `migrations/1789095456.sh`, a lock-screen fingerprint PAM repair. Today that is an add/add conflict with `quattro`, which still holds the Mise cleanup under that name. This PR moves the Mise cleanup away, so after it lands #11322 merges without a conflict. The fingerprint repair then carries an id already marked complete on the edge and development accounts listed below:

```text
quattro + #12174 + #11322 (local merge), real bin/omarchy-migrate --pending
Synthetic accounts; the fingerprint migration itself was not run

account marker state             pending migrations
no 1789095456.sh marker          1789095456.sh (fingerprint repair)
1789095456.sh marker present     none (the repair is skipped)
```

The marker is held by three groups:
- accounts that ran migrations from `quattro` during the PTL window;
- accounts that ran the Mise cleanup under `1789095456` since #11336 merged;
- accounts provisioned while either migration shipped.

That is the #12173 collision again, for a third migration.

**Impact:** this PR is correct as it stands. But merging it removes the conflict that currently exposes the reuse, and #11322 has no discussion of it. If #11322 then merged with its current id, the fingerprint repair would silently not run for those accounts.

**Suggested change:** no change to this PR. #11322 needs a fresh migration id. This cross-reference is intended to make the dependency visible on both PRs.

**Root cause (context):** `bin/omarchy-dev-add-migration` names a new migration after HEAD's commit time (`git log -1 --format=%cd --date=unix`). The `quattro` merge commit of #11263 has committer time exactly `1789095456`. Branches started from that commit (#11336, #11322, and the closed #11345 and #11346) all received that id. The PTL migration also carries the id, but how it got it was not established. A helper that uses the current time would avoid this, and a merge-time check against migration names already used in the target branch's history would catch the rest. That fits better in a separate issue than in this PR.

---

## Review information

**Test scope:** Source and history review of head `72c37a91` and current `quattro` `3faafba2`, plus open PRs that touch either migration id, the migration runner or these tests. Local merges of this PR with current `quattro`, #13365 and #11322 were built for testing. Both repository tests and the Mise cleanup scenarios ran in an isolated sandbox. The scenarios ran each tree's real `bin/omarchy-migrate` against synthetic homes, with mise 2026.9.4, including a trust-via-settings variant. All other migrations were pre-marked complete, and the PTL and provisioning markers were created directly. The #11322 effect was checked with `--pending` only. Its migration (sudo, `/etc/pam.d`) was not executed. Base tests were not re-run.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis, Opus 5.5 Xhigh technical review and final fact check, GPT 6 Sol Xhigh search for related issues, Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.
